big: Two friends, same age, both want ₹1 crore of cover. One buys a plain term plan. The other buys a plan that returns the premiums at the end. Their yearly bills are very different.

lines: My agent says the return of premium plan is better, because I get the money back.
You do get back what you paid, but that costs a lot more each year. Let us compare with made-up numbers.

rows: Money back if you survive (₹ lakh)
alt: Two sets of bars comparing total premiums paid and money back for two plans
caps: Made-up premiums: ₹10,000 a year for plain term and ₹30,000 for return of premium.
Over thirty years the plain plan costs ₹3 lakh and the other ₹9 lakh.
The second plan gives back its ₹9 lakh at the end, with no growth on it.
The extra ₹6 lakh of premium would have been available to invest elsewhere.

intro: Plain terms for a term plan.
rows: Pays the sum assured if you die within the term, nothing if you survive
How many years the cover lasts, ideally until earning years end
An add-on, such as accidental death or critical illness, for extra premium
note: A term plan should run until the earner's income years end, not just a few years.

q: Rohan buys a 30-year term plan and survives the term. What does the plan pay him?
opts: The sum assured, since the term has ended
Nothing, since a plain term plan pays only on death
All his premiums back, along with some interest
Half of the sum assured, as a loyalty benefit
why: The sum assured goes to the nominee on death in the term, not to him on survival.
A plain term plan pays only if the insured dies within the term, so survival pays nothing.
Premium refunds apply only to return of premium plans, and they carry no interest.
There is no loyalty benefit in a plain term plan. It pays only on death in the term.

q: Meena is 30 and works until 60. She buys a 10-year term plan to save on premium. What is the problem?
opts: Cover for ten years is always enough for a family
The plan pays nothing during its first ten years in force
The premium rises every single year until she turns 60
Cover ends at 40, though her family may rely on her until 60
why: A short term leaves the family uncovered in years when she is still earning.
A term plan pays on death within the term, including the first ten years.
Term premiums are usually fixed for the whole term and do not rise every year.
Cover should last until her earning years end, so a ten-year term leaves a long gap.

q: Rohan compares two plans for ₹1 crore of cover. One refunds premiums at the end and costs three times as much. What should he think about?
opts: The extra premium could be invested, so compare cover cost
Take the refund plan, since money back is always the better deal
The cheaper plan will certainly not pay out at claim time
Both plans must cost the same, since the cover is equal in size
why: The extra premium buys the refund, so compare cover cost and what else the money could do.
The refund is only his own premiums returned, so the higher cost is a real trade-off.
Price alone does not decide claim payment. Terms and honest disclosure do.
Prices differ because of the refund feature, so the plans do not cost the same.

q: What is a rider on an insurance policy?
opts: A person who sells the policy on behalf of the insurer
A rule that lets you skip premiums in any tough year
An add-on like accidental death cover, for extra premium
A clause that raises the cover by itself every single year
why: A person who sells policies is an agent or distributor, not a rider.
Riders do not let you skip premiums. Missing premiums can lapse a policy.
A rider adds a benefit such as critical illness or accidental death for an extra premium.
Automatic yearly increases are a different feature. Riders are chosen add-ons.

pts: A plain term plan pays only on death in the term, and costs the least.
Choose a term that lasts until your earning years end.
A return of premium plan costs much more for the same cover.
